newsitem.title: UK: Physical tin interest stirred by price weakness.
newsitem.headline: Physical tin interest stirred by price weakness.

text.p: Current weakness in tin prices, allied to currency considerations, has sparked some physical interest and enquiries resulting in solid physical premiums.

But the level of actual business does not as yet suggest that the market is due for a turnaround as many consumers are still biding their time and there is producer selling above the market, traders added.
"People are looking for lower levels, perhaps down to $5,800, but it is a good time to buy nevertheless. There is a lot of enquiry around," one trader said.

On the London Metal Exchange (LME) on Tuesday, three months tin prices dropped to a low of $5,910 a tonne, close to the lowest levels for 1-1/2 years. Today, prices were holding around $5,930/40 a tonne. "If it drops under $5,900 there are sell-stops in place. The next level will be $5,850 or even $5,800," another trader said.
Since late-August tin prices have been falling steadily from highs just above $6,300, with the market responding more to copper's weakness than its own fundamentals.
Buyers have been adopting a "wait-and-see" attitude, but Tuesday's weakness resulted in Jan/Feb 1997 end-user offtake on the Continent.
"The D-mark was strong against the dollar and that helped not only the Germans but also other Europeans. Here (in the UK), we've seen enquiry certainly, but not so much business," a trader said.

Premiums, meanwhile, are holding at reasonably steady levels in Rotterdam. There is a broad $40/50 premium over LME cash in place for "three nines" metal with additional costs then added on for particular origins.
The premiums for "low-lead" tin are higher, as many end-users are opting for this metal, and range from $150 to $200, they said.
But although tin is nicely-balanced at present with inventories at comfortable levels, if there is an upswing in prices and offtake there will be pressure on premiums.
"The problem is that metal is moving into Liverpool, which is basically a dumping ground for the Malaysians," one said.

Total LME warehouse stocks stand at 10,075 tonnes, of which 4,065 tonnes is in Rotterdam and 4,185 tonnes is stored in Liverpool. If there is offtake in Europe, lifting costs from the UK warehouse are higher than in Rotterdam, so there is the possibility of short-term tightness.
